description: Betty Friedan, NOW, the ERA fight and the Stonewall riots — gender and sexuality politics 1960s–70s.
content_html:
The Feminine Mystique and the Women’s Movement

In 1963, Betty Friedan published The Feminine Mystique. The book argued that educated middle-class women were trapped by an unspoken cultural expectation — what Friedan called “the problem that has no name” — that their only true fulfilment lay in marriage, motherhood and housekeeping. The book sold three million copies in three years and is credited with sparking the second wave of American feminism. It gave a name to a widespread but previously unarticulated dissatisfaction.

The year 1963 also saw tangible progress on policy. President Kennedy’s President’s Commission on the Status of Women (established 1961) reported in 1963, documenting systematic workplace discrimination. The same year, the Equal Pay Act was signed — the first federal law banning sex-based wage discrimination. It required equal pay for “equal work” but was narrowly defined and left many inequalities untouched.

Key Fact

The Equal Pay Act (1963) required equal pay for equal work but was narrowly defined. Title VII of the Civil Rights Act (1964) banned employment discrimination on grounds of sex as well as race, and created the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission — but enforcement was initially weak.

NOW and the Equal Rights Amendment

In 1966, Betty Friedan, Pauli Murray and others founded the National Organisation for Women (NOW). NOW combined mainstream lobbying with legal challenges: it filed complaints with the EEOC about sex discrimination, campaigned against “help wanted — male” job advertisements, and pushed for the Equal Rights Amendment (ERA). The ERA — a constitutional amendment stating that “equality of rights under the law shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any state on account of sex” — had been introduced in Congress in various forms since 1923. In 1972, Congress passed it and sent it to the states for ratification.

The ERA’s ratification campaign ultimately failed. Phyllis Schlafly’s STOP ERA campaign organised effective opposition, arguing that the ERA would remove beneficial protections for women — including exemption from military draft — and lead to unisex toilets and other outcomes many Americans found alarming. By 1982, the ERA had failed to win ratification from the required 38 states. Schlafly’s success demonstrated that the women’s movement faced genuine organised opposition, not merely inertia.

In late June 1969, police raided the Stonewall Inn, a gay bar in Greenwich Village, New York City. Such raids were routine — homosexuality was illegal in most states. What was different was the response: bar patrons, including Marsha P. Johnson and other prominent figures, fought back against the police over several nights. The Stonewall riots are widely regarded as the founding moment of the modern LGBT rights movement. Within a year, LGBT organisations had formed across the country and the first Gay Pride marches were held. In 1973, the American Psychiatric Association removed homosexuality from its list of mental disorders.

Roe v Wade and the Limits of Progress

In 1972, the Supreme Court’s Eisenstadt v Baird ruling guaranteed single people the same right to contraception that married couples had received in Griswold v Connecticut (1965). The following year, in January 1973, the Supreme Court ruled 7–2 in Roe v Wade that the Constitution protected a woman’s right to an abortion in the first trimester. The decision was framed in terms of privacy, not sex equality, and immediately triggered a powerful conservative counter-movement. By the mid-1970s, the feminist movement had achieved significant legal gains but faced fierce organised opposition on multiple fronts.

Pauli Murray was a Black civil rights lawyer and activist who helped design the legal strategy connecting the ban on sex discrimination to the Civil Rights Act. She had been arguing since the 1940s that the same constitutional arguments used against racial discrimination applied equally to sex discrimination. She was a co-founder of NOW and served on the President’s Commission on the Status of Women. Murray’s career demonstrates that the civil rights and feminist movements were not separate: many activists, especially Black women, worked in both simultaneously and saw the struggles as inseparable.

Key Fact

Phyllis Schlafly’s STOP ERA campaign argued the amendment would harm women by removing protective legislation and subjecting them to military conscription. By 1982 it had failed to win ratification from the 38 states needed — the first major legislative defeat of second-wave feminism.
exam_tip_html: This lesson has a lot of specific legislation: know the Equal Pay Act (1963), Title VII (1964), the ERA (passed Congress 1972, ratification failed 1982) and Roe v Wade (January 1973). The exam requires you to assess the ‘impact’ of feminism — show both gains (legal discrimination banned, EEOC created, Roe v Wade) and limits (ERA defeated, enforcement weak, economic inequality persisted). The Stonewall riots 1969 is explicitly named in the specification — make sure you can explain what happened and its significance as the start of the LGBT rights movement. For Schlafly, show she was a major historical force, not an afterthought.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Betty Friedan’s Feminine Mystique (1963), the Equal Pay Act (1963), Title VII (1964) and the founding of NOW (1966) built the legal and organisational foundations of second-wave feminism.
  • The ERA passed Congress in 1972 but Phyllis Schlafly’s STOP ERA campaign successfully blocked ratification; Roe v Wade (1973) secured abortion rights but triggered a lasting conservative counter-movement.
  • The Stonewall riots of June 1969 marked the beginning of the modern LGBT rights movement, and by 1973 the American Psychiatric Association had removed homosexuality from its list of disorders.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: Identifies a specific feature with accurate detail, e.g. the book argued that educated middle-class women were trapped by an unspoken cultural expectation that their only fulfilment lay in marriage and housekeeping, which Friedan called 'the problem that has no name.' Secure: Correct identification with some detail. Developing: Vague reference to a book about women. Emerging: No relevant content.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the impact of the feminist movement on legislation in the years 1963 to 1972.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Mastering: Two well-supported features, e.g. (1) the Equal Pay Act 1963 required equal pay for equal work, the first federal law against sex-based wage discrimination; (2) Title VII of the Civil Rights Act 1964 banned employment discrimination on grounds of sex and created the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. Secure: Two features with some detail. Developing: One feature with detail, or two without. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Equal Rights Amendment failed to be ratified despite passing Congress in 1972.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains multiple reasons with specific evidence — Schlafly's STOP ERA campaign organised effective grassroots opposition; she argued the ERA would harm women (remove military draft exemption, end protective legislation); many states were conservative; the ERA's ratification window expired in 1982. Shows how these factors combined. Secure: Two or more reasons with evidence. Developing: Describes the failure without explaining causes. Emerging: Brief or inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the Stonewall riots of 1969 were significant for the development of LGBT rights in the USA.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons, e.g. (1) the riots marked the first time LGBT people collectively fought back against routine police harassment, shifting from passive endurance to assertive protest; (2) within a year, LGBT organisations had formed across the country and the first Gay Pride marches were held, creating an organised movement that previously had not existed. Secure: Two reasons with evidence. Developing: Two reasons without clear development. Emerging: One weak point.

practice_questions.text: How significant was NOW in advancing women's rights in the USA between 1966 and 1974?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Balanced analysis — NOW was significant because it combined lobbying, litigation and public campaigns; filed EEOC complaints; pushed Title VII enforcement; campaigned for ERA. But places it in context: Equal Pay Act and Title VII predated NOW; Friedan's book and the Commission had laid the groundwork; ERA failed; Roe v Wade came through Supreme Court rather than NOW campaigns. Compares NOW's significance to other factors. Integrated judgement. Secure: Clear argument with evidence. Developing: Describes NOW without weighing significance. Emerging: Narrative only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the development and impact of feminist movements in the USA in the years 1963 to 1974.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained analytical essay covering The Feminine Mystique (1963), the Equal Pay Act (1963), Title VII (1964), founding of NOW (1966), ERA (1972 and ratification failure), Roe v Wade (1973), Stonewall (1969). Reaches an integrated judgement about what changed and what remained limited. Well-chosen evidence throughout. Secure: Several developments with evidence and some sustained analysis. Developing: Describes events with limited structure. Emerging: Brief narrative.

knowledge_checks.q: What was the central argument of Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique?
options: That women should enter political office
That educated women were trapped by expectations of marriage and housekeeping as their only fulfilment
That women should have equal military service
That civil rights legislation applied equally to gender

knowledge_checks.q: In what year did the Supreme Court rule in Roe v Wade?
The National Organisation for Women (NOW) was founded in _____ by Betty Friedan and others.
The Stonewall riots of June 1969 began when police raided the Stonewall Inn, a gay bar in _____ Village, New York City.
Match each legislation to what it did:
right: Passed Congress but failed ratification by 1982
Required equal pay for equal work between sexes
Banned employment discrimination on grounds of sex

flashcard_questions.q: When was The Feminine Mystique published and who wrote it?
What did the Equal Pay Act 1963 require?
flashcard_questions.a: Equal pay for equal work — the first federal law banning sex-based wage discrimination.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Title VII of the Civil Rights Act 1964 do for women?
flashcard_questions.a: Banned employment discrimination on grounds of sex and created the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.
1966, by Betty Friedan, Pauli Murray and others.

flashcard_questions.q: When did the ERA pass Congress?
flashcard_questions.a: 1972 — but it failed to win ratification from the required 38 states by 1982.

flashcard_questions.q: Who led the STOP ERA campaign?

flashcard_questions.a: June 1969 protests in New York City when LGBT people fought back against a police raid, marking the start of the modern LGBT rights movement.

flashcard_questions.q: When was Roe v Wade decided?
flashcard_questions.a: January 1973 — the Supreme Court ruled 7–2 that the Constitution protected abortion rights in the first trimester.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is Pauli Murray significant to both the civil rights and feminist movements?
flashcard_questions.a: A Black lawyer who connected anti-racial-discrimination arguments to sex discrimination; co-founded NOW and shaped the legal strategy behind Title VII.

glossary_terms.definition: Author and feminist activist who published The Feminine Mystique (1963) and co-founded the National Organisation for Women (NOW) in 1966.

glossary_terms.term: President's Commission on the Status of Women
glossary_terms.definition: A federal advisory body chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt that documented workplace discrimination against women and recommended legislative remedies.
The National Organisation for Women, founded in 1966, which campaigned for equal rights for women through legislation, litigation and political pressure.

Conservative activist who founded the STOP ERA campaign in 1972, arguing that the amendment would harm women by removing protections and potentially requiring women to be drafted into military service.
A series of spontaneous protests by LGBT people against a police raid on the Stonewall Inn in New York City in late June 1969, widely regarded as the beginning of the modern LGBT rights movement.
